title: Non-Government Assistance - Canadian SR&ED Tax Glossary
description: Understand the impact of Non-Government Assistance and inducements on your R&D expenditure pool in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.

Canada’s research and development (R&D) tax incentive framework, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, is the largest single source of federal government support for industrial innovation in the country, delivering over $4 billion in tax incentives annually to more than 18,000 claimant businesses (with federal baseline tax expenditure projections rising from $4.7 billion in 2025–2026 to $6.4 billion by 2030–2031)1.

Between December 2024 and November 2026, the Canadian R&D tax regime underwent its most substantial legislative transformation in more than a decade9. On March 26, 2026, Bill C-15 received Royal Assent, enacting the legislative reforms proposed in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and the November 4, 2025 Federal Budget with retroactive application to taxation years beginning after December 15, 20249. Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million (increasing the maximum annual federal cash refund on current expenditures for eligible corporations to $2.1 million, as noted by tax practitioners), expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extended access to the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restored the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 20244. Concurrently, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 2026, providing upfront project eligibility determinations within eight weeks10, while Federal Budget 2026 (accompanied by a Notice of Ways and Means Motion updated November 5, 2026) proposed a $930 million five-year expansion to bring regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) protection costs into the SR&ED program for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day17. Provincially, British Columbia permanently aligned its 10% credit with the federal $6 million limit, ECPC expansion, and capital expenditure restoration16, whereas Quebec eliminated its legacy R&D tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing them with the consolidated Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which provides a 30% refundable rate on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialisation expenditures exceeding an exclusion threshold21.
1. Legislative Architecture and the 2025–2026 Statutory Reforms
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Structure under the Federal Income Tax Act

The federal SR&ED program is a statutory tax entitlement governed by the federal Income Tax Act (ITA) and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR) rather than a discretionary grant5. It delivers tax relief through two distinct, sequential statutory mechanisms that interact across taxation years1:

items: The Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (ITA Section 37): Under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may accumulate allowable current expenditures—and, for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, eligible capital expenditures—incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada in a dedicated expenditure pool5. The taxpayer may deduct any portion of the positive balance of this pool when computing net income from business for the current taxation year, or carry the undeducted pool balance forward indefinitely to deduct against business income in any future taxation year5.

The SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITA Sections 127 and 127.1): Under subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1) of the ITA, a claimant earns an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a statutory percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of its "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year4. Under section 127.1, qualifying claimants that cannot fully utilise the ITC to reduce Part I federal income tax otherwise payable may receive 100% (on current expenditures within the expenditure limit) or 40% (on capital expenditures or basic-rate expenditures for eligible claimants) of the unused credit as a cash refund4. Unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years to offset Part I tax payable in those years1.

body.text: To prevent a taxpayer from receiving both an income deduction and a tax credit on the same dollar of outlay, any SR&ED ITC deducted from Part I tax payable or refunded in cash in a taxation year reduces the taxpayer's section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the immediately following taxation year pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(e) of the ITA (or in the same fiscal period in the case of a partnership pursuant to paragraph 96(1)(e.1))5.
1.2 Enactment of Bill C-15 (Royal Assent: March 26, 2026)

The 2025–2026 federal SR&ED reforms progressed through two fiscal announcements before being enacted into law by Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 20269. First, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024) proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3 million to $4.5 million, widening the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% enhanced rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs4. Second, Federal Budget 2025 (tabled November 4, 2025) increased the proposed annual expenditure limit further from $4.5 million to $6 million, effective for the same taxation years beginning after December 15, 20245. Bill C-15 codified both stages into the Income Tax Act on March 26, 20269.

body.text: 1.3 Federal Budget 2026 Commercialisation and IP Protection Expansion Proposals

Building upon the enactment of Bill C-15, Federal Budget 2026 (with its Notice of Ways and Means Motion to Amend the Income Tax Act updated November 5, 2026) proposed a further expansion of the SR&ED program to support the commercialisation and protection of Canadian R&D17. Applicable to taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day, Budget 2026 commits $930 million over five fiscal years ($25 million in 2026–2027, $200 million in 2027–2028, $245 million in 2028–2029, $225 million in 2029–2030, and $235 million in 2030–2031 and ongoing) to expand eligible SR&ED activities and outlays across two new fronts17:

items: Regulatory and Certification Testing and Validation: Budget 2026 expands SR&ED eligibility to cover tests, technological validations, and studies conducted to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining the initial approval or certification necessary to commercialise a new or improved product or process17. These regulatory validation activities must directly relate to an underlying project that is eligible under existing SR&ED rules, and they permit claimants to claim the standard categories of eligible SR&ED expenditures—wages and salaries, materials, contracting costs, overhead costs, and machinery and equipment17.

Intellectual Property (IP) Registration and Maintenance Costs: Under prior law, the CRA treated patent filing and IP protection fees as ineligible administrative or legal expenses incurred to protect, rather than conduct, SR&ED25. Budget 2026 proposes to include costs reasonably incurred to obtain and maintain protection for eligible IP developed in the course of an eligible SR&ED project17. Eligible IP instruments comprise patents, certificates of supplementary protection, plant breeders' rights, and copyrighted software under relevant Canadian legislation or equivalent legislation in a foreign jurisdiction17. Eligible outlays include expenses incurred to prepare and file an application for eligible IP protection (provided supporting activities such as application preparation are conducted in Canada), periodic maintenance fees payable to keep IP rights in force, and administrative fees payable to domestic or foreign IP offices17. Costs incurred to enforce IP rights (such as infringement litigation) or costs not directly connected to securing and maintaining IP rights remain ineligible, and if a taxpayer subsequently disposes of IP for which SR&ED IP-protection support was claimed, recapture rules will apply to claw back the related SR&ED deduction and investment tax credit amounts17.

body.text: Note that while earlier policy discussions in Canada considered a separate preferential "patent box" corporate tax regime, Chapter 1 of Federal Budget 2026 did not introduce a patent box tax rate; instead, it delivered commercialisation support through this $930 million SR&ED expansion, a $1 billion allocation over six years (starting in 2028–2029) to the Strategic Response Fund (formerly the Strategic Innovation Fund), renewed support for the NRC-IRAP Clean Technology Initiative, and targeted amendments to the Patent Act regarding mandatory registration of patent ownership changes and minimum requirements for patent demand letters17.
2. Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Technical Eligibility Framework
2.1 The Four Pillars and Seven Exclusions of Subsection 248(1)

The statutory foundation for all federal and harmonized provincial R&D tax incentives is the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act5. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls within one of four qualifying limbs5:

items: Paragraph (a) – Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view5.
Paragraph (b) – Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view5.

Paragraph (c) – Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto5. As confirmed by the CRA, experimental development is the most commonly claimed category of SR&ED work in Canada5.

Paragraph (d) – Eligible Support Work: Work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where that work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer5. These eight support categories are exhaustive38. Support work does not meet the definition of SR&ED on its own; it qualifies only when carried out specifically to support eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development5.

body.text: Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) designate seven excluded categories of work that cannot be claimed for SR&ED tax incentives (subject to the prospective Budget 2026 inclusions for initial regulatory certification testing and IP protection)5:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion5;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes5;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities5;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas5;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process5;
Paragraph (j): Style changes5; and
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection5.

body.text: In its Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentives (published August 13, 2021, and updated July 5, 2022), the CRA emphasizes that distinguishing between eligible support work under paragraph (d) and excluded work under paragraphs (e) to (k) turns on the purpose for which the activity was performed5. For instance, routine data collection or testing conducted to support normal business operations such as quality assurance is excluded under paragraphs (f) and (k), whereas data collection or testing carried out specifically to evaluate a hypothesis in an experimental development project qualifies as eligible support work under paragraph (d)5.
2.2 Evolution of CRA Eligibility Guidance: From IC 86-4 to the "Why" and "How" Requirements
While the statutory text of subsection 248(1) has remained stable since 1992, the CRA’s administrative framework for evaluating work eligibility has evolved through four historical milestones41:
Historical Evolution of Administrative Guidance (1985–2021)

Prior to 1985, Revenue Canada administered R&D claims under Interpretation Bulletin IT-43941. Following taxpayer feedback that IT-439 was inadequate, the Department of Finance announced in the May 23, 1985 Budget Papers (Securing Economic Renewal) that the regulatory definition would be amended to introduce the term "experimental development", clarifying that projects involving only routine engineering or routine development were excluded41. On March 4, 1986, the Department of Finance confirmed to Revenue Canada that eligible R&D must embody scientific or technological advancement, involve scientific or technological uncertainty, and be conducted in a systematic and organised manner41. This led to the publication of Information Circular 86-4 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development) in 1986 (revised as IC 86-4R3 in 1994), followed by the December 2, 1992 legislative clarification confirming that incremental improvements in experimental development qualify41. In 1998, Justice Bowman's landmark decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839) synthesized IC 86-4R3 and subsection 248(1) into five sequential questions, which the CRA adopted in its 2012 Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (revised on April 24, 2015, to replace "scientific method" with "systematic investigation or search", and archived on August 13, 2021)5. Finally, in August 2021, the CRA replaced the 2012 policy with the current Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, which structure the subsection 248(1) analysis around two mandatory pillars: the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement5.
The "Why" Requirement: Scientific or Technological Uncertainty and Advancement

The "Why" requirement governs the objective of the work: it must be undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement by resolving a scientific or technological uncertainty5.

A scientific or technological uncertainty exists when it is uncertain whether a given objective or result can be achieved, or how to achieve it, because of an insufficiency of available scientific or technological knowledge5. The baseline of available knowledge encompasses both the claimant's internal resources and publicly available knowledge accessible to competent professionals in the field5. Characteristics indicating that technological knowledge is insufficient include situations where existing design methods are not applicable, requirements or specifications conflict with existing standards, too many variables or unknowns interact, operating parameters lie outside normal ranges, the nature of the problem evolves unpredictably, or interlocking technical constraints prevent a standard solution5. While economic or cost targets alone do not create technological uncertainty, attempting to meet cost targets under rigid physical or performance constraints may impose a genuine technological uncertainty5. Furthermore, the CRA's SR&ED Glossary explicitly recognizes system uncertainty—a form of technological uncertainty that arises during the integration of technologies whose individual components or sub-systems are well known, but whose combined interactions cannot be predicted5.

Recognizing a technological uncertainty is the starting point of SR&ED, and attempting to resolve that uncertainty constitutes an attempt to achieve technological advancement—defined as the generation or discovery of conceptual knowledge (such as theories or predictive models, rather than mere factual measurements) that advances the understanding of technology5. Acquiring existing knowledge or know-how through employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge or patents does not satisfy the "Why" requirement5. Similarly, if an uncertainty is ignored or circumvented by adopting an existing workaround based on available knowledge, the work is ineligible5. Conversely, success or failure in achieving the project's commercial or technical objective is irrelevant: a project that fails to achieve its desired physical outcome remains fully eligible if its purpose was to generate knowledge that advances the understanding of science or technology5.
The "How" Requirement: Systematic Investigation or Search

The "How" requirement governs the methodology of the work: it is not enough to follow standard engineering procedures, intuitive trial and error, or a systematic business plan5. Instead, the claimant must execute a systematic investigation or search encompassing four distinct elements5:

items: Formulating a Hypothesis: Generating an idea, proposed method, or potential solution consistent with known scientific or technological facts to serve as the starting point for resolving the uncertainty5;

Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Testing the hypothesis through structured experiment or analysis (defined in the SR&ED Glossary as the detailed examination of information against available knowledge using models, graphs, statistics, tables, diagrams, mathematical formulas, or computer programs to differentiate parts of a whole, determine their attributes, or explain their relationships), allowing the hypothesis to evolve as test findings emerge5;
Developing Logical Conclusions: Formulating logical conclusions based on the empirical or analytical results obtained5; and
Maintaining Contemporaneous Evidence: Keeping dated records and evidence generated as the work progresses to substantiate the investigation5.

body.text: 2.3 Shop-Floor SR&ED: Production Runs and Asset Development Policies

When experimental development takes place in an industrial or manufacturing facility rather than an isolated laboratory, claimants must apply two specific CRA policies to segregate eligible SR&ED from excluded commercial operations5:
1. SR&ED During Production Runs Policy (ED+EP vs. ED+CP)

The SR&ED During Production Runs Policy governs experimental development (ED) performed during the operation of equipment or processes in a commercial manufacturing environment5. The policy distinguishes between two production run contexts based on the nature of the output and the technical risk involved5:

items: ED+EP (Experimental Development where the Output is Experimental Production): Refers to a production run (such as a pilot plant run or a dedicated experimental trial) whose output is experimental production (EP) required specifically to verify whether technological advancements are achievable or whether SR&ED objectives have been met5. Evidence of technical risk in an ED+EP context includes specific experimental operating instructions prepared in advance, senior management authorization for runs involving risk of equipment damage or process instability, close monitoring by additional technically qualified personnel, yield losses above normal commercial tolerances, and production quantities commensurate solely with experimental needs5. In an ED+EP context, the salaries of directly engaged employees (including supervised non-specialised machine operators) and the full cost of materials consumed or transformed in the required experimental production run are allowable SR&ED expenditures5. Any output beyond what is strictly needed to evaluate the SR&ED is excess production, and all labour, material, and overhead costs attributable to excess production are disallowed5.

ED+CP (Experimental Development Simultaneous with Commercial Production): Refers to experimental development conducted in conjunction or simultaneously with a normal commercial production run5. Under ED+CP, all salaries, input materials, and overhead attributable to normal commercial production are strictly excluded; only the additional (incremental) costs of employee wages and extra materials consumed or transformed directly because of the experimental development during the run are allowable5.

body.text: 2. SR&ED While Developing an Asset Policy (Pilot Plants, Prototypes, and Custom Products)

The SR&ED While Developing an Asset Policy classifies assets designed, constructed, or tested in a commercial environment into four categories: (1) Pilot Plants (non-commercial scale facilities isolated from normal business operations and developed for the primary purpose of carrying out SR&ED over their useful life to evaluate hypotheses, establish process formulae, or test unproven equipment), (2) Commercial Plants, (3) Prototypes, and (4) Custom Products / Commercial Assets (assets built to meet customer specifications for subsequent sale or commercial use)5. Constructing duplicate copies of a prototype after successful testing to build inventory is excluded commercial work; however, if multiple duplicate copies of a prototype are constructed prior to commercial production solely for destructive or validation testing commensurate with the needs of the SR&ED, their construction costs (labour, materials, and overhead) qualify as materials consumed or transformed and are claimed in the taxation year when testing is completed (not when the copies are constructed)5. When developing a custom product or commercial asset where only certain components involve SR&ED, non-affected commercial components are ineligible; if apportioning expenses between the SR&ED and commercial portions is difficult through standard accounting, the CRA permits the Alternative Approach (usable under both the Traditional and Proxy methods), which estimates allowable SR&ED expenditures as5:

Allowable SR&ED expenditures = (total actual costs of developing the custom product or commercial asset − estimated costs that would usually be associated with the construction of the asset if the technology had already existed) + estimated costs of materials transformed
3. Federal SR&ED Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, Phase-Outs, and Pool Mechanics
3.1 Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures: Additions, Reductions, and Restrictions

The pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) of the ITA is calculated on Part 3, Section C of Form T661 (Lines 429 to 470) as a continuous running balance that does not expire5. Because the CRA maintains the pool as an aggregate running balance, the specific taxation year in which a pooled expenditure was originally incurred is not tracked once added to the pool5.
Statutory Additions and Reductions to the Section 37 Pool
Under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is increased each taxation year by5:

items: Paragraph 37(1)(a): Allowable expenditures of a current nature incurred in the year on SR&ED carried on in Canada—directly undertaken by the taxpayer (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i)), performed by a contractor on behalf of the taxpayer (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), or paid as third-party payments to Canadian resident corporations or approved research entities (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii))5;
Paragraph 37(1)(b): Eligible SR&ED capital expenditures (restored by Bill C-15 for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, reported on Line 390 of Form T661)4;
Paragraph 37(1)(c): Repayments made by the taxpayer in the year of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the section 37 pool (Line 445)5;
Paragraph 37(1)(c.1): Amounts included in the taxpayer's income from business in a preceding taxation year by virtue of paragraph 12(1)(v) due to a negative pool balance5; and
Paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and 37(1)(c.3): Amounts added to Part I tax payable in the preceding taxation year because of an SR&ED ITC recapture or a partnership ITC recapture excess amount (Line 453)5.

body.text: Conversely, the section 37 pool is reduced each taxation year by5:

items: Paragraph 37(1)(d): All government assistance and non-government assistance (as defined in subsection 127(9)) in respect of SR&ED expenditures that, at the taxpayer's filing-due date for the year, the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive (Lines 429, 431, and 432)5;
Paragraph 37(1)(d.1): Provincial super-allowance benefit amounts5;

Paragraph 37(1)(e): Federal SR&ED ITCs deducted from Part I tax payable and/or refunded in cash in the preceding taxation year (Line 435), plus proceeds of disposition of SR&ED capital property up to the undeducted expenditure balance for that property (Line 440)5; and

Paragraphs 37(1)(f) and 37(1)(f.1): Amounts deducted from the pool under subsection 37(1) in preceding taxation years (reflected in the prior-year closing pool balance on Line 450) and amounts deducted in respect of insolvency under section 61.3 in preceding years5.

body.text: If pool reductions exceed pool additions and the opening balance at the end of a taxation year, the resulting negative pool balance must be included in computing the taxpayer's business income for that year under paragraph 12(1)(v), which resets the pool balance to nil for the following year via paragraph 37(1)(c.1)5.
Statutory Restrictions on the Section 37 Pool
Four critical statutory restrictions govern the section 37 pool:

items: Prohibition on Acquiring Rights in SR&ED (ITA Subsection 37(4) & ITR Paragraph 2902(c)): Under subsection 37(4) (and Regulation 2902(c) for ITC purposes), no deduction may be made under subsection 37(1) for any expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (such as purchasing a patent, buying existing technology rights, or paying an additional sum under a separate contract to buy IP rights from a contractor), as established in Halak v. Minister of National Revenue (89 DTC 531)5.

Related Corporations, Exclusive Economic Zone, and Foreign Research (ITA Subsections 37(1.1), 37(1.3), and 37(2)): Under subsection 37(1.1), SR&ED performed by a corporate claimant is deemed related to a business of the claimant if it relates to a business actively carried on by a related corporation (determined without reference to control by right under paragraph 251(5)(b))5. Under subsection 37(1.3), SR&ED conducted in the waters or airspace of Canada's exclusive economic zone is deemed carried on in Canada5. Conversely, expenditures for research carried on outside Canada (other than permissible employee salaries within the subsection 37(1.5) limit) cannot be added to the section 37 pool or earn an ITC, and may only be deducted as current business expenses under subsection 37(2)5.

Loss Restriction Events / Acquisition of Control (ITA Subsection 37(6.1) and Paragraph 37(1)(h)): If a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (or a trust has a new majority-interest beneficiary), a deemed taxation year-end is triggered immediately before the event and the undeducted section 37 pool is reduced to nil5. The pre-acquisition pool balance may be reinstated and deducted in a subsequent taxation year only if the specific business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent of the taxpayer's income for that subsequent year (before any section 37 deduction) from that same business or a similar business5.

Priority Over Charitable Donations (ITA Subsection 37(5)): Where an outlay qualifies as both an SR&ED expenditure under section 37 and a charitable donation under section 110.1 (corporations) or section 118.1 (individuals), subsection 37(5) mandates that the amount must be deducted as an SR&ED expenditure and not as a charitable gift5.

body.text: Statutory Definitions of Claimant Categories

Under subsection 125(7) of the ITA, a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) is a private corporation that is a Canadian corporation other than a corporation controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (de jure or de facto), by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), by one or more corporations listed on a designated stock exchange, or by any combination thereof—including under the paragraph 125(7)(b) "hypothetical shareholder" rule, which deems all voting shares owned by non-residents and public corporations to be owned by a single hypothetical person52.
For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, subsection 127(9) of the ITA defines an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) as either4:

items: A corporation that: (i) is resident in Canada; (ii) is a public corporation, or would be a public corporation if the words "designated stock exchange in Canada" in paragraph (a) of the definition of "public corporation" in subsection 89(1) were read as "designated stock exchange"; (iii) is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons; and (iv) would not, if each share of its capital stock owned by a non-resident person (as determined, absent actual knowledge, based on publicly available information including securities filings made before the year) were owned by a single particular person, be controlled by that particular person13; or

An "eligible subsidiary", defined as a corporation resident in Canada of which not less than 90% of the issued shares of each class of its capital stock is owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more corporations that are ECPCs under paragraph (a) of that definition35.

body.text: Under subsection 127.1(2), a "qualifying corporation" is a CCPC throughout the taxation year whose taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations for their last taxation year ending in the preceding calendar year, and grossed up to 365 days under subsection 127.1(4) if a short taxation year was less than 51 weeks) does not exceed its qualifying income limit4. Note that a CCPC whose prior-year taxable income exceeds its qualifying income limit ("CCPC other than a qualifying or excluded corporation") still receives a 100% refund of its 35% enhanced ITC on current expenditures (and a 40% refund on capital expenditures) up to its expenditure limit under subsection 127.1(2.01); it merely loses the 40% refund on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures exceeding the expenditure limit4. An "excluded corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) is a corporation controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by (or related to) one or more tax-exempt entities under section 149, His Majesty in right of a province, a Canadian municipality, or any other public authority; an excluded CCPC earns the 35% ITC up to its limit, but its refund rate on current expenditures is limited to 40%4. Finally, SR&ED expenditures incurred by a Crown-owned corporation (other than a Prescribed Federal Crown Corporation under Income Tax Regulations section 7100) are excluded from earning an ITC because such corporations are exempt from Part I tax5.
3.3 Expenditure Limit Formulas and Phase-Out Mechanics
1. The $6 Million Expenditure Limit and Taxable Capital / Revenue Phase-Out (Post-Dec 15, 2024)

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC is $6,000,000 (increased from $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024)4. Associated CCPCs must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit and allocate it among group members on Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsection 127(10.3)5. Similarly, ECPCs must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit among all group members included in their consolidated financial statements13. Short taxation years and multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year also reduce the expenditure limit proportionally13.

Under the Bill C-15 rules for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit phases out linearly between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 (replacing the pre-December 16, 2024 phase-out range of $10,000,000 to $50,000,000)4:

items: For CCPCs (Taxable Capital Test): The expenditure limit begins to decrease when the taxable capital employed in Canada for the previous taxation year (combined across all associated corporations) reaches $15,000,000, and becomes nil ($0) at $75,000,0004.

For ECPCs and Electing CCPCs (3-Year Average Annual Revenue Test): For an ECPC, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit begins to decrease when the consolidated group's average annual revenue over the previous three fiscal years exceeds $15,000,000, and becomes nil ($0) starting at $75,000,0004. Under the post-December 15, 2024 rules, a CCPC or group of associated CCPCs may also elect using the prescribed form to calculate its expenditure limit reduction using this same 3-year average annual revenue method instead of taxable capital4.

body.text: 2. The Qualifying Income Limit Formula (ITA Subsection 127.1(2))

To determine whether a CCPC qualifies as a "qualifying corporation" (entitled to a 40% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures exceeding its expenditure limit or allocated from a partnership), its prior-year taxable income (combined across associated corporations) must not exceed its qualifying income limit4. Under subsection 127.1(2) of the ITA, the qualifying income limit formula is4:

items: For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024: Qualifying income limit = $500,000 × ($40,000,000 − A) ÷ $40,000,000 where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is ≤ $10,000,000, and in any other case is the lesser of $40,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $10,000,000 (phasing out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000)4.

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024: Qualifying income limit = $500,000 × ($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000 where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is ≤ $15,000,000, and in any other case is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000 (phasing out between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000)4.

body.text: 3.4 Special Rules for Partnerships (SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy)

Because a partnership is not a "person" or taxpayer under the Income Tax Act (though its net income is computed at the partnership level as if it were a separate person), paragraph 96(1)(e.1) and subsection 127(8) impose five specialized rules documented in the CRA's SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy5:

items: Mandatory Full Deduction of the Section 37 Pool (No Carryforward): A partnership cannot carry forward a pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to a subsequent fiscal period5. The entire balance of the partnership's section 37 pool at the end of its fiscal period must be deducted in full in computing the partnership's net income or loss for that year5.

Same-Year Pool Reduction for Allocated ITCs: Whereas an individual or corporation reduces its section 37 pool by ITCs claimed or refunded in the prior taxation year, any SR&ED ITC allocated by a partnership to its partners reduces the partnership's section 37 pool in the same fiscal period in which the allocation occurs, regardless of whether the partners actually apply the credit against Part I tax or receive a cash refund5. Conversely, any partnership ITC recapture excess amount added to the Part I tax of partners increases the partnership's section 37 pool in the subsequent year (paragraph 37(1)(c.3))5.

15% Basic Rate Ceiling and Prohibition on NAL Transfers: Under subsection 127(8) and paragraph 127(9)(b), a partnership's SR&ED ITC is calculated strictly at the 15% basic rate, even if all members of the partnership are CCPCs or qualifying corporations5. Furthermore, partnerships cannot transfer or receive qualified expenditures under subsection 127(13) (Form T1146)5.
Disallowance of ITCs and SR&ED Losses for Limited Partners and Specified Members:

Loss Restriction for Limited Partners: A partnership loss created or increased by deducting the partnership's section 37 SR&ED pool cannot be claimed by a limited partner5. The deductible business loss of a limited partner is reduced by the lesser of the partnership's section 37 pool deduction and the total partnership loss, and the disallowed amount is permanently lost (it cannot be claimed by other partners, does not become a limited partnership loss or non-capital loss, and does not adjust the limited partner's adjusted cost base)5.

Prohibition on Allocating ITCs to Specified Members: Under subsection 127(8), no SR&ED ITC may be allocated to a "specified member" of the partnership—defined in subsection 248(1) as any limited partner or any passive general partner who was not regularly, continuously, and substantially actively engaged in the partnership's business activities (other than financing) or carrying on a similar business during the fiscal period5. Any ITC share that cannot be allocated to specified members is reallocated to the active general partners (non-specified members) based on what is reasonable having regard to their investment (including debt obligations) in the partnership5. An active general partner receiving such reallocated ITCs may elect on Form T932 under subsection 127(8.4) to renounce all or part of those reallocated ITCs so that the renounced credits are extinguished without reducing the partnership's section 37 deductible expenditure pool5.

Ineligibility of Partner Salaries: A member of a partnership cannot be an employee of the partnership for income tax purposes; any salary or wages paid to a partner is treated by the CRA as a distribution of partnership income and cannot be claimed as an SR&ED salary or wage expenditure51.

body.text: 3.5 Carryback, Carryforward, and Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits

items: Application, Carryback, and Carryforward Rules: Earned SR&ED ITCs must first be applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year under subsection 127(5)4. Where a taxpayer claims a refundable ITC under section 127.1, the refunded amount is deemed by subsection 127.1(3) to have been deducted under subsection 127(5), reducing the ITC pool available for carryover4. Any remaining unapplied ITC may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (limited to the lesser of the unused current-year ITC and the excess of Part I tax payable over ITCs available in that prior year) or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years, subject to acquisition-of-control streaming restrictions1.

Recapture of SR&ED ITCs (ITA Subsections 127(27) to 127(36)): Under the Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy and subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA, if a taxpayer (or a non-arm's length transferee) sells or converts to commercial use within 20 taxation years a property whose cost was previously claimed as a qualified SR&ED expenditure—specifically materials transformed, SR&ED capital depreciable property (acquired before 2014 or after December 15, 2024), Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), or a physical component acquired under an SR&ED contract—the ITC earned on that property is recaptured and added directly to the taxpayer's Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion (reported on Schedule T2SCH31 for corporations or Form T2038(IND) for individuals)4.

The recapture amount under subsection 127(27) is the lesser of: (1) the actual SR&ED ITC earned in respect of the particular property, and (2) the historical percentage rate used in calculating the SR&ED ITC on that property multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (if disposed of to an arm's length person) or the fair market value (FMV) of the property (if converted to commercial use or disposed of to a non-arm's length person)5.

Under subsection 127(32), "cost" for recapture purposes cannot exceed the amount paid by the claimant to acquire the property from another person and excludes internal labour or overhead incurred by the claimant to maintain, modify, or transform the property48. Consequently, if a claimant builds a prototype component in-house, recapture applies only to the cost of the raw materials transformed (e.g., $135,000 of transformed materials) and not to the in-house salaries or overhead; whereas if the claimant orders the custom component from an arm's length supplier under contract (e.g., $10,000 manufacturing/development cost plus $2,000 profit = $12,000), the entire $12,000 contract price paid to acquire the physical part is subject to recapture48.

For Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), because only 25% (First Term) or 50% (First and Second Term combined) of the capital cost qualified for the ITC, recapture is limited to the lesser of the total SUE ITC obtained and the ITC calculated on 25% or 50% of the proceeds of disposition or FMV5. Disposing of or licensing intellectual property (IP) generated by SR&ED does not trigger recapture under subsection 127(27) where the IP accrued to the claimant as it was generated (though under the Budget 2026 proposals, disposing of IP for which new IP-protection expenses were claimed will trigger recapture of those specific IP-protection tax incentives)17.

body.text: 4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Overhead Calculation Methodologies
4.1 Salary or Wages (SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, Updated January 28, 2025)

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, "salary or wages" means the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act (Sections 5 to 8)—corresponding to gross employment remuneration reported on an employee's T4 slip—excluding superannuation or pension benefits and retiring allowances5. To be claimed, salary or wages must be incurred for SR&ED under subsection 37(8) and paid within the taxation year or within 180 days of the end of the taxation year under subsection 78(4)23.
1. Employee Eligibility Categories: Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method
The scope of claimable employee remuneration depends on whether the claimant elects the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method23:

items: Directly Engaged in SR&ED (Claimable under Both Proxy and Traditional Methods): Refers strictly to hands-on work determined by the actual tasks performed by the employee rather than job title5. Eligible directly engaged tasks include: (1) hands-on experimentation and analysis; (2) the eight statutory categories of support work (engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research); (3) tasks performed by non-specialised employees (such as operating a machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into a machine) when supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications; (4) direct technical supervision of employees performing SR&ED (requiring a significant technological background and excluding general administrative management) and technical input into SR&ED contract administration and coordination; (5) technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the tax year (such as personnel assignment, job priorities, technological strategy development, and material quality selection); (6) technological feasibility studies relating to SR&ED projects carried out; and (7) preparing technical documentation for internal use5. Under Income Tax Regulations subsection 2900(5), if a directly engaged employee spends all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of their working time on eligible SR&ED duties, 100% of their eligible salary or wages qualifies5. When prorating partial SR&ED involvement, the CRA uses total time available for work (typically approximately 250 working days per year, assuming 5 working days per week less 11 statutory holidays)23.

Directly Undertaking, Supervising, or Supporting SR&ED, and Clerical/Administrative Staff (Traditional Method Only): Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the ITA and paragraphs 2900(2)(b) and 2900(2)(c) of the Income Tax Regulations, claimants electing the Traditional Method may also claim on Line 360 (Overhead and Other Expenditures) of Form T661 the salary or wages of clerical, administrative, purchasing, or human resources staff who provide a service to SR&ED employees, provided the wages satisfy both the "directly related" test and the "incremental" test (the cost would not have been incurred had the SR&ED prosecution not occurred)5. Under the Proxy Method, all clerical, administrative, and indirect support staff wages are covered by the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and cannot be claimed separately23.

body.text: 3. Specified Employee Limitations (ITA Subsections 37(9) and 37(9.1); ITR Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8))

Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a "specified employee" is an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a "specified shareholder" owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation23. Specified employees are governed by two distinct statutory ceilings tied to the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan23:

items: Direct SR&ED Salary/Wages Ceiling (Line 305 / Line 309 – ITA Subsections 37(9) and 37(9.1)): All bonuses and profit-based remuneration paid to a specified employee are strictly disallowed23. Furthermore, under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum allowable SR&ED salary or wages claimable for a specified employee is limited to 5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the employee was a specified employee23. If a specified employee performs SR&ED for two or more associated corporations, no amount may be claimed unless the associated corporations file an allocation agreement on Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) sharing a single 5 × YMPE limit5.

Proxy Salary Base Ceiling (Part 5, Lines 850–860 of Form T661 – ITR Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8)): When computing the salary base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), subsection 2900(7) of the Income Tax Regulations restricts the amount included for a specified employee to the lesser of11:

75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (combining both SR&ED and non-SR&ED work, and excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits under sections 6 and 7, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year)31; or

2.5 × A × (B ÷ 365), where A is the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends and B is the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for days during the year when the individual was not a specified employee)31. Under Regulation 2900(8), if a specified employee is employed by multiple associated corporations, a single 2.5 × YMPE ceiling must be shared across the associated group55.

body.text: 4. Permissible Salary or Wages for SR&ED Performed Outside Canada (ITA Subsections 37(1.5) and 37(9.1))

Under subsections 37(1.5) and 37(9.1) of the ITA, a claimant may claim on Lines 307 and 309 of Form T661 a limited portion of salary or wages ("permissible salary or wages") for SR&ED work performed outside Canada, subject to the statutory limit calculated on Form T661, only if all five of the following criteria are met5:

items: The SR&ED work outside Canada was performed directly by an employee of the claimant and not by a contractor or subcontractor36;
The employee who performed the work was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred36;
The work was related to the business of the claimant36;
The work performed outside Canada was an integral part of, and solely in support of, an SR&ED project carried out by the claimant in Canada23; and
The salary or wages paid are not subject to an income or profits tax from another country23.

body.text: 4.2 Overhead Calculation Methodologies: Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method

Under subsection 37(10) of the ITA and the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, a claimant must choose either the Proxy Method (electing on Line 160 of Form T661) or the Traditional Method (choosing Line 162) when filing Form T661 for each taxation year5. The selection is made annually and is irrevocable for that taxation year once Form T661 is submitted (defaulting to the Traditional Method if no election is made on the initial filing)5.
1. The Proxy Method (ITA Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) & ITR Subsections 2900(4) to 2900(10))

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not specifically identify, track, or claim actual overhead and indirect support expenses on Form T6615. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional substitute amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the SR&ED salary base pursuant to Income Tax Regulations subsection 2900(4) (reduced from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013 to 55% for 2014 and all subsequent calendar years)5. The PPA is entered on Line 502 of Form T661 to earn the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC), but because the PPA is a notional amount rather than an actual outlay, neither the PPA nor the actual overhead expenses it replaces can be added to the section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (actual overhead costs remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the ITA)5.

To prevent single-purpose R&D corporations with minimal overhead from claiming a notional PPA that exceeds their actual total non-SR&ED operating deductions, Income Tax Regulations subsection 2900(6) imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA, calculated by the formula55:
PPA ≤ A − B − C

where A is the total of all business deductions claimed by the taxpayer for the taxation year (including cost of goods sold), B is the sum of specific statutory deductions claimed under sections 20 (such as Capital Cost Allowance [CCA] and interest), 24, 26, 30, 32, 37 (the SR&ED pool deduction claimed on Line 460), 66 to 66.8, and 104, and C is the total expenditure incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (building rent)55.
2. The Traditional Method (ITA Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) & ITR Subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3))

Under the Traditional Method, the claimant enters 0 on Line 502 and instead specifically identifies, tracks, allocates, and substantiates each actual overhead expenditure on Line 360 of Form T661, adding those actual overhead costs to both the section 37 deductible pool and the qualified expenditure pool for ITC purposes5. To qualify under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (II) of the ITA and Income Tax Regulations subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3), each overhead outlay must be either all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) attributable to the prosecution (or the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution) of SR&ED in Canada, or directly attributable—meaning both directly related and incremental (it would not have been incurred if the SR&ED prosecution or SR&ED premises/facilities/equipment had not existed)5.

As detailed in the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022), eligible Line 360 overhead under the Traditional Method includes: (i) salaries/wages of clerical and administrative staff providing a direct, incremental service to SR&ED employees; (ii) the employer's share of related benefits (CPP/QPP, EI, WSIB/CNESST, approved pension, medical/dental/optical plans) and retiring allowances for hands-on SR&ED employees only (related benefits, retiring allowances, training, and travel for clerical/administrative staff are disallowed as an indirect link); (iii) expenses related to selecting and hiring SR&ED personnel; (iv) lease costs of equipment used <90% of the time for SR&ED (proportional to SR&ED usage); (v) incremental costs of telephone, cellular, and Internet services; (vi) travel and lodging in Canada to perform testing at a customer location or for SR&ED training in Canada; (vii) incremental utilities (electricity, water, fuel) and maintenance/upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment (note that fixed-cost maintenance contracts generally fail the incremental test); (viii) periodical subscriptions; (ix) incremental waste disposal during an active SR&ED project (disallowed once the SR&ED activity has finished); (x) fees paid to volunteers in clinical studies; and (xi) health and safety expenses5. Conversely, under Income Tax Regulations section 2902, prescribed expenditures—including fees paid for preparing SR&ED claims, costs to attend conventions or conferences, and interest expenses—are strictly excluded from earning an ITC even if they are directly related and incremental5.
3. Treatment of Cloud Computing (AWS, Azure, GCP) and Software Licences/Subscriptions

In Canadian accounting and tax practice, a frequent compliance issue for software, artificial intelligence, and product design claimants is the treatment of cloud computing costs (such as AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud infrastructure) and software subscriptions (such as CAD or simulation SaaS licences)11:

items: Exclusion from "Materials Consumed or Transformed": Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, "materials for SR&ED" must be raw materials or physical substances that at a given moment compose the body of a thing on which SR&ED is performed5. As CPA tax practitioners emphasize, cloud computing subscriptions and SaaS software licences do not compose the physical body of a product and therefore are not materials consumed5.

Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method Treatment: Under the Proxy Method, general cloud computing costs and software subscriptions constitute overhead that is already represented by the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Regulation 2900(4), meaning they cannot be claimed separately11. Under the Traditional Method, however, cloud computing and software subscription expenses that are segregated from production infrastructure, directly related to SR&ED experimentation, and incremental (incurred solely because of the SR&ED work) can be claimed as actual overhead on Line 36011. Thus, as CPA guidance notes, salary-heavy teams with modest infrastructure costs benefit from the 55% Proxy Method, whereas compute-heavy AI or data analytics firms whose incremental cloud spend exceeds 55% of their SR&ED salary base should evaluate electing the Traditional Method11.

Post-December 15, 2024 Rules for Dedicated Bandwidth and Software Tooling: Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026) and SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), for expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024: (1) the lease of dedicated bandwidth (other than general-purpose office equipment) used ≥90% (or >50% at a 50% inclusion rate) for SR&ED qualifies as an equipment lease expenditure under the Proxy Method15; and (2) computer software or software licences purchased as a tool to perform SR&ED (such as computer-aided design software, provided the software is not incorporated into a final commercial product) may qualify as an SR&ED capital expenditure (if providing enduring benefit beyond one year and meeting the ≥90% intent test) or as a current lease expenditure depending on the legal nature of the licence contract5.

body.text: 4.3 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Materials for SR&ED Policy)

Under both the Traditional Method (ITR paragraph 2900(2)(a)) and the Proxy Method (ITA subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V)), claimants may claim the cost of materials either consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (purchased from Canadian or foreign suppliers, provided the outlay is paid within 180 days of fiscal year-end)5. The allowable cost is the laid-down cost—the original acquisition invoice cost plus all reasonable costs incurred to bring the material to the location and condition required for the SR&ED5. Materials purchased for future SR&ED can be claimed only in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed5.

items: Materials Consumed (Line 320 of Form T661): Materials that are absorbed, used up, broken down into small pieces, destroyed, or rendered virtually valueless (retaining less than 10% of their original cost) as a result of the SR&ED work5. If 90% or more of the cost of a material is consumed in SR&ED, the entire cost (100%) is allowable on Line 320 and is not subject to ITC recapture5.

Materials Transformed (Line 325 of Form T661): Materials that have been changed or incorporated into another material or product as a result of the SR&ED and retain some value (such as a resale or scrap value greater than 10% of original cost) to the claimant or another party5. If the transformed materials or resulting product are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 taxation years, SR&ED ITC recapture applies under subsections 127(27) to (36)5.

Animals, Plants, Water, Energy, and Lab Supplies: Animals and growing plants involved in SR&ED (along with animal feed, fertilizers, pesticides, herbicides, and fungicides) qualify as materials consumed, limited to incremental costs if conducted alongside commercial production5. General laboratory supplies that do not compose the body of a thing being researched (such as test tubes, pipettes, vials, beakers, flasks, cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, and used lubricants) and general utilities (electricity, natural gas, oil, washing/utility water, and boiler feed water) do not qualify as materials (they are claimable only as Line 360 overhead under the Traditional Method)5. The only exceptions are process water (water that enters a process as a chemical reactant governed by chemical equations and becomes part of an intermediate or final product, not used in commercial production) and energy directly required for endothermic reactions (in chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical, biotechnology, metallurgical refining, cement, glass, ceramics, or plastics forming processes where the physical material retains the energy input)5.

body.text: 4.4 Subcontractor Payments, Non-Arm's Length Transfers, and Third-Party Payments
The Income Tax Act applies distinct eligibility and ITC inclusion rules to arm's length SR&ED contracts, non-arm's length SR&ED contracts, and third-party payments5.
1. Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts (Line 340 of Form T661)

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) of the ITA and the Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy, where a claimant contracts an arm's length performer to conduct SR&ED on behalf of the claimant in Canada:

items: 100% Deductible Pool / 80% ITC Inclusion: 100% of the eligible contract expenditure enters the section 37 deductible pool, but under subsection 127(9) (effective after 2012), only 80% of the arm's length contract expenditure qualifies for the SR&ED ITC (20% of Line 340 is subtracted on Line 529 of Form T661)27.

Canadian Performance and "Taxable Supplier" Requirement: The SR&ED work must be carried out in Canada by the ultimate performer (foreign contract work cannot be claimed on Form T661 and earns no ITC, though it is deductible as a general business expense under subsection 37(2))40. Furthermore, to earn an ITC, the contract amount must be paid or payable to a "taxable supplier"—defined in subsection 127(9) as a person resident in Canada, a Canadian partnership, or a non-resident person/partnership carrying on business through a permanent establishment in Canada (defined in Income Tax Regulations section 8201)5. Payments to a non-taxable supplier are deducted on Line 528 and earn no ITC27.

IP Ownership, Support-Only Contracts, and Preventing Double Claims: Work is performed "on behalf of" the payer when the contract terms as a whole show that the payer controls the work and typically retains exclusive ownership of the resulting SR&ED and IP25. To prevent duplicate ITC claims, the payment received or receivable by the arm's length performer is a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) that reduces the performer's own qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18)40. If a payer contracts out only support work (paragraph 248(1)(d)) to an arm's length performer, the payer can claim the contract expenditure provided the support work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of underlying basic/applied research or experimental development performed by or on behalf of the payer; however, the arm's length performer cannot claim SR&ED expenditures for a support-work-only contract because support work on its own does not meet the definition of SR&ED40.

The Look-Through Rule (ITA Subsections 37(14) and 37(15)) and Prepaid/Unpaid Rules: Under subsection 37(14) (the look-through rule), a payer's SR&ED contract expenditure must be reduced by any related expenditure of the performer that is not of a current nature, and under subsection 37(15) the performer must notify the payer in writing of that reduction without delay if requested, or no later than 90 days after the end of the calendar year40. Payments for contracted SR&ED not yet performed at year-end are disallowed as prepaid expenses under subsection 18(9), and contract amounts unpaid 180 days after year-end must be deducted on Line 520 under subsection 127(26) (and added back at 80% on Line 500 in the subsequent year when paid)27.

body.text: 2. Non-Arm's Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Line 345) and Form T1146 Transfers
When a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) performer (defined under section 251 of the ITA):

items: No Direct ITC for the Payer: The contract amount paid to the NAL performer is reported on Line 345 and enters the payer's section 37 deductible pool, but it is not a qualified expenditure and earns 0% ITC for the payer directly31.

Performer Claim or Form T1146 Transfer (ITA Subsections 37(13) and 127(13)): For the NAL performer, the amount received from the NAL payer is not a "contract payment" under subsection 127(9) and does not reduce the NAL performer's qualified expenditures40. Moreover, under subsection 37(13), if the NAL performer performs only support work, that support work is deemed to be SR&ED provided it would qualify as SR&ED if performed directly by the NAL payer40. The NAL performer may either claim the ITC itself or file a joint agreement on Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) under subsection 127(13) to transfer all or part of its qualified expenditures (up to the contract price) to the NAL payer (reported on Line 508 for the transferee and Line 544 for the transferor)5.

Anti-Avoidance Rule on Intermediaries (ITA Subsection 127(24)) and NAL Cost Adjustments (Subsections 127(11.6)–(11.8)): Under subsection 127(24), if a payer (Corp A) contracts an arm's length intermediary (Corp B) who subcontracts the work to a party dealing at non-arm's length with Corp A (Subco C), and the main purpose is to allow Corp A to claim a qualified expenditure, Corp A's expenditure is disallowed while the payments to Corp B and Subco C retain their character as contract payments—resulting in none of the corporations earning an ITC5. Additionally, where a claimant buys goods or non-SR&ED services from a NAL supplier, subsections 127(11.6) to 127(11.8) limit the qualified expenditure to the Adjusted Selling Cost or Adjusted Service Cost (eliminating any intercompany profit on Lines 538–542 of Form T661)5.

body.text: 3. Third-Party Payments (Line 370 and Form T1263)

body.text: 4.5 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, capital expenditures and equipment lease costs—which had been excluded from SR&ED since January 1, 2014—are once again eligible for SR&ED tax incentives when acquired (and available for use) or incurred after December 15, 2024, governed by three updated CRA policy documents5:
1. Dedicated SR&ED Capital Expenditures (SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy, Updated June 29, 2026)

Depreciable property (excluding a building, a leasehold interest in a building, land, inventory, or intangibles such as goodwill, and excluding software intended to be incorporated into a final product) acquired and available for use (under subsection 13(27) of the ITA) after December 15, 2024, qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 of Form T661 (with the 10 most expensive properties and their SR&ED operating time percentages reported on Lines 262 and 263) if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended either5:

items: That the property would be used during all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%, or more than 90%) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the performance of SR&ED in Canada5; or

That all or substantially all (≥90%, or more than 90%) of its value would be consumed in the performance of SR&ED in Canada (such as when rapid technological obsolescence occurs or when the property is destroyed during testing)5.

body.text: The CRA evaluates acquisition intent by examining the claimant's past practices with similar property and contemporaneous planning documents (project plans, business cases, funding requests, and contingency plans)5. Capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 are 100% deductible in the section 37 pool (and therefore must not be included on Schedule 8 for Capital Cost Allowance [CCA])5. For ITC purposes, new depreciable property earns the 35% enhanced ITC (or 15% basic ITC), with the 35% ITC on capital expenditures being 40% refundable in cash4. However, used equipment (property used, or acquired to be used or rented, for any purpose before acquisition by the claimant) is a prescribed expenditure under Income Tax Regulations paragraph 2902(b): while used property meeting the ≥90% test can be deducted in the section 37 pool, it does not qualify for an SR&ED ITC5. When SR&ED capital property is later sold, Line 440 of Form T661 reduces the section 37 pool by the lesser of the proceeds of disposition and the undeducted pool balance for the property (with any excess proceeds up to original capital cost included in income as recaptured CCA on Schedule T2SCH1), while also triggering SR&ED ITC recapture under subsection 127(27)5.
2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy, Updated May 22, 2026)

Where new depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, does not meet the ≥90% ASA test for dedicated SR&ED capital property, it may qualify for SR&ED ITCs on Line 504 of Form T661 as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) under subsection 127(9) if it is used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) of its actual operating time for SR&ED in Canada5. To qualify as SUE, the property must be new, must not be general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF), and must not be Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Income Tax Regulations subsection 2900(11) (property intended at acquisition to be used for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing facility/line and intended over its expected useful life to be used primarily for non-SR&ED commercial purposes; note that equipment used in pilot plants is never PDP)5. Unlike PDP (which is tested on intended use at acquisition), SUE is tested on actual operating time across two cumulative periods5:

items: First Term SUE: Evaluated from the date the property becomes available for use until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition5. If used >50% for SR&ED during that first period, 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (excluding section 21 capitalized interest, determined without reference to subsections 13(7.1) and 13(7.4), and adjusted for NAL transactions under subsection 127(11.6) and assistance) is deemed to be a qualified SR&ED expenditure5.

Second Term SUE: Evaluated from acquisition until the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition5. If the property qualified as First Term SUE and was used >50% for SR&ED across the second period, an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (for a cumulative 50% across both terms) qualifies for the SR&ED ITC5.

body.text: 3. Equipment Lease Expenditures (SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy, Updated June 8, 2026)

Lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada (excluding building rent under paragraph 37(8)(e) unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance under Regulation 2903, and requiring a reasonable allocation where a lease covers both a building and equipment) qualify as current SR&ED expenditures15:

items: Under the Traditional Method: If leased equipment is used 90% or more (ASA) of the time for SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 350 (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)); if used less than 90% for SR&ED, the lease cost is claimed as overhead on Line 360 in an amount proportional to the percentage of time used for SR&ED, provided the lease is directly related and incremental (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) and Regulation 2900(2)(c))15. Costs to lease land incurred after December 15, 2024, are also claimable as Line 360 overhead under the Traditional Method if ASA or directly attributable to SR&ED15.

Under the Proxy Method: Excluding general-purpose office equipment or furniture (GPOEF) and leased land (which cannot be claimed under the Proxy Method), if leased equipment is used 90% or more (ASA) of its operating time for SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 350 (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)); if used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) of its operating time for SR&ED, exactly 50% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 355 (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)); if used 50% or less, 0% is claimable15. Claimants must maintain lease agreements, invoices, cancelled cheques, and contemporaneous logbooks establishing actual SR&ED operating time15.

Cash Refund Comparison (Leasing vs. Purchasing Equipment): Because eligible equipment lease costs are current expenditures, a CCPC or ECPC within its $6 million limit receives a 100% cash refund on the 35% enhanced ITC earned on leased equipment, whereas purchasing the same equipment outright as a capital expenditure yields a 40% cash refund on the 35% ITC (with the remaining 60% of the credit carried forward as a non-refundable ITC)4.
