body.text: 5.2 Deep-Dive on Key Provincial Reforms and Mechanics
1. Quebec’s 2025–2026 Overhaul: The Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)

Announced in the March 25, 2025 Budget Speech by Quebec’s Minister of Finance and detailed in Revenu Québec and Ministère des Finances guidance, Quebec replaced its fragmented R&D tax credit system with the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation) for taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 20256.

To consolidate tax support for innovation, Quebec eliminated seven legacy tax measures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 (though corporations, individuals, and trusts with taxation years beginning before March 26, 2025, could still claim the legacy credits using Forms RD-222-V, RD-1029.7-V, RD-1029.8.6-V, RD-1029.8.9.03-V, and RD-1029.8.16.1-V)21: (1) the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages of Researchers (R&D); (2) the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium; (3) the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium; (4) the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research; (5) the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services; (6) the industrial design component of the Design Tax Credits (retaining only the fashion design component); and (7) the Tax Holiday for Foreign Researchers and Experts21.

Under the new CRIC regime (claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR alongside Form RD-222, Form RD-1029.8.EN for associated-group expenditure limit allocation, and Form RD-1029.8.PR for the pre-commercialisation component, reported under Codes 112 and 113 on the CO-17 corporate return)6:

items: 30% and 20% Refundable Rates Across All Corporate Sizes: Eligible corporations operating a business in Quebec with an establishment in the province earn a 100% refundable tax credit equal to 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold, and 20% on all qualified expenditures above that $1,000,000 limit, regardless of the corporation's asset size21.

Modified Exclusion Threshold: Qualified expenditures for the taxation year must exceed an exclusion threshold equal to the greater of: (1) $50,000, or (2) the sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold (calculated using the basic personal amount of the Quebec personal income tax system for each employee, adjusted to reflect the actual percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialisation activities)21.

Eligible R&D and Pre-Commercialization Activities: While the R&D component (Code 112) is harmonized with the federal definition of SR&ED (and the CRA continues to perform the scientific review of R&D work), the CRIC adds a Pre-Commercialization Component (Code 113) for activities that constitute a continuation of R&D undertaken in Quebec by or on behalf of the corporation21. Eligible pre-commercialisation activities comprise: (a) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification to commercialise an innovation; (b) product design (development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials); and (c) quality control activities, provided they relate specifically to implementing a quality control system required to obtain initial approval or certification21.

Qualified Expenditures and Anti-Cumulation Rules: Qualified CRIC expenditures include 100% of direct employee salaries and wages, 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors for contracts carried out in Quebec, 50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, eligible research consortium, or eligible university entity, and capital expenditures (property acquisition costs) for new or used depreciable property (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings) acquired for R&D or pre-commercialisation in Quebec21. A corporation cannot combine the CRIC with another Quebec tax credit (such as the Tax Credit for Investment and Innovation [C3i]) on the same expenditure, nor can it claim the CRIC on property used in a large investment project holding a tax-holiday certificate22.

body.text: 2. Alignment vs. Holdouts Across Other Provinces
As analyzed in provincial tax commentary (such as Copoint and Axscope as of October–November 2026) and official CRA provincial schedules7:

items: British Columbia (Full Alignment & Permanence): In BC Budget 2026, British Columbia removed the statutory sunset date on the 10% BC SR&ED Tax Credit (Form T666), making the credit permanent, and expressly aligned with the federal Bill C-15 reforms for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—adopting the $6,000,000 refundable expenditure limit (up from $3,000,000), the $15,000,000–$75,000,000 prior-year taxable capital phase-out range, access to the 10% refundable credit for Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and the restoration of capital expenditures7.

Ontario (Separate Rules Maintained): Ontario has not adopted the federal $6 million limit or capital expenditure restoration for its 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC, Schedule 566 & Schedule 31), which remains capped at $3,000,000 of qualifying current expenditures and phases out between $500,000 and $800,000 of prior-year federal taxable income or $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year specified paid-up capital7. Ontario also provides the 3.5% non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC, Schedule 508 & Schedule 31) (carryback 3 years, carryforward 20 years) and the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC)7. A corporation may waive or renounce the OITC or ORDTC in writing within 6 months of its tax year-end (or on an amended return)7.

Alberta (Independent IEG Framework): On June 30, 2026, Alberta published updated guidance confirming that its Innovation Employment Grant (IEG, AT1 Schedule 29 & Form AT4970) continues to operate under its existing provincial parameters—providing an 8% refundable grant on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base spending level (the prior 2-year average) and an enhanced 20% refundable grant (8% base + 12% incremental) on spending above the 2-year base, up to a maximum annual expenditure cap of $4,000,0007.

Saskatchewan (Targeted Provincial Expansion): Rather than adopting the $6 million federal limit or ECPC rules, Saskatchewan doubled the refundable expenditure threshold under the 10% Saskatchewan R&D Tax Credit (Schedule 403) for Saskatchewan CCPCs from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 for qualifying expenditures incurred on or after December 16, 2024 (while retaining a $1,000,000 annual cap on total combined refundable and non-refundable credits per corporation)7.

Manitoba, Atlantic Provinces, and Yukon: Manitoba (Schedule 380) continues to provide a 15% credit (half [7.5%] refundable and half [7.5%] non-refundable for in-house R&D, or 100% [15%] refundable for R&D under contract with a qualifying Manitoba research institute, with 100% inclusion for eligible Manitoba educational institution contracts) and already recognized eligible capital expenditures for depreciable property (excluding buildings) prior to the federal restoration7. Nova Scotia (Schedule 340), New Brunswick (Schedule 360), Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule 301 / Form T1129), and Yukon (Schedule 442 / Form T1232) all provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit with no dollar expenditure cap (plus an additional 5% [20% total] in Yukon for payments to Yukon University, and with Newfoundland and Labrador uniquely not reducing eligible expenditures by government or non-government assistance other than GST/HST input tax credits)7.

body.text: 6. Interaction with Government Assistance, Grants, and Stacking Arithmetic
6.1 Statutory Rules on Government and Non-Government Assistance (ITA Paragraph 37(1)(d), Subsections 127(9) and 127(18)–(20), and Paragraph 12(1)(x))

As set out in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, "government assistance" means assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority (including Crown corporations, foreign governments, and indirect government funding passed through a non-profit organization per paragraph 12(1)(x)) in the form of a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance, excluding the federal SR&ED ITC46. "Non-government assistance" means any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) (read without reference to subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(v) to (vii))46.

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18) to 127(20) of the ITA, government and non-government assistance that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year reduces both the section 37 deductible pool (Lines 429–432) and qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes (Lines 513–517) on a project-by-project basis down to nil (assistance on a funded project cannot reduce the qualified expenditures of a separate unfunded project; any excess assistance above a project's SR&ED expenditures is included in income)5. Non-arm's length group members performing SR&ED on the same assisted project may allocate the assistance reduction among themselves using Form T1145 under subsection 127(20)5. When a claimant subsequently repays government or non-government assistance (or a contract payment), the repayment increases the section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(c) (Line 445) and earns an ITC in the year of repayment under paragraphs 127(9)(e.1) and (e.2) (Line 560) at the historical ITC rate that applied when the assistance originally reduced the claim; however, because a repayment is not a "qualified expenditure", the resulting ITC is non-refundable in the year of repayment (available for Part I tax offset, 3-year carryback, or 20-year carryforward)5.
Treatment of Provincial Tax Credits and Wage Subsidies under the Proxy Method
A critical mechanical distinction applies when a claimant elects the Proxy Method:

items: Provincial R&D Tax Credits Attributable to the 55% PPA: Under subsection 127(18), the entire provincial or territorial R&D tax credit (whether refundable or non-refundable, unless renounced by the filing-due date) reduces federal qualified SR&ED expenditures on Line 513—including the portion of the provincial credit earned on the federal 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)31. However, because the PPA is a notional amount that is never added to the section 37 deductible pool, the portion of the provincial R&D tax credit that relates to the PPA does not reduce the section 37 pool on Line 429; instead, that PPA-related provincial credit portion must be included directly in business income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the taxation year it is received46. Similarly, under Quebec's legacy R&D salary credit (for taxation years beginning before March 26, 2025), any provincial credit earned on indirect R&D support salaries that did not qualify under the federal Proxy Method did not reduce the federal section 37 pool and was instead included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) when received21.

Wage Subsidies and Salary Grants (CRA CEWS/TWS Guidance & NRC-IRAP): As confirmed in the CRA's Guidance: How the Canada Emergency Wage Subsidy Affects SR&ED Claims (updated October 11, 2024) and grant stacking guidelines, government wage subsidies or salary grants (such as NRC-IRAP or legacy CEWS/TWS) received or receivable for time spent by employees directly engaged (or directly attributable under the Traditional Method) in SR&ED constitute government assistance5. However, under the Proxy Method, the 55% PPA in Part 5 of Form T661 is computed on the unreduced gross SR&ED salary base (e.g., in the CRA's published example, $16,800 of gross SR&ED salary generates a full 55% PPA of $9,240 before the government wage subsidy is deducted from total qualified expenditures in Part 4)5.

body.text: 6.2 Major Federal Grant Programs: NRC-IRAP and the Strategic Response Fund

items: National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC-IRAP):

Program Streams and Funding Data: Delivered through a network of over 250 Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs), NRC-IRAP provides prospective, non-repayable R&D contributions to incorporated Canadian SMEs71. According to industry grant data compiled by GrantCompass (as of November 2026), NRC-IRAP provided $393.1 million to 3,136 SMEs in FY2024–2025 (with a median disclosed contribution of $75,000, typical first-time awards ranging from $75,000 to $200,000, and Large Value Contributions up to $10 million reaching $1M+ fewer than 10 times per year) across four active streams71: (1) Core IRAP (general technology R&D across all sectors); (2) the Clean Technology Stream (formed in June 2024 when NRC-IRAP absorbed the mandate of Sustainable Development Technology Canada [SDTC], and proposed for renewal in Federal Budget 2026); (3) Defence Industry Assist (DI Assist) (launched in January 2026 with $244.2 million for dual-use technologies in cybersecurity, autonomous systems, and advanced materials); and (4) AI Assist (supporting generative AI and deep learning solutions)18.

Reimbursement Rates and 75% Stacking Cap: As summarized by GrantCompass, NRC-IRAP reimburses up to 80% of direct technical employee salary costs and up to 50% of arm's length subcontractor costs, subject to a 75% Total Government Assistance Cap across all combined federal, provincial, and municipal funding sources (including IRAP, SR&ED, and provincial grants/credits)71.
Strategic Response Fund (Formerly Strategic Innovation Fund – SIF):

Initially launched in 2017 as the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF), the program was renamed the Strategic Response Fund in Federal Budget 2026, which proposed $1 billion over six years, starting in 2028–2029, to fund large-scale R&D and innovation projects across key sectors including artificial intelligence, agri-food, bio-manufacturing, and clean technologies18.

Judicial Precedent on Repayable Government Contributions: Even when a federal contribution under the Strategic Innovation Fund, Strategic Response Fund, or legacy SADI/ACOA programs is structured as an unconditionally repayable loan, the Federal Court of Appeal held in Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada (2014 FCA 196) and CAE Inc. v. The Queen (2022 FCA 178, leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada denied in 2023) that interest-free or concessional government loans lacking ordinary commercial lending terms constitute "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x)—reducing qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar in the year received46.

body.text: 7. Governing Authorities, Filing Procedures, Prescribed Forms, and Audit/Review Protocols
7.1 Dual Governance and the Strict 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline

The federal SR&ED program is jointly governed by the Department of Finance Canada (responsible for legislative policy under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations) and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) – Business Tax Incentives Directorate (located at the Enterprise Building, 13th Floor, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa, ON K1A 0L5, which administers all federal SR&ED claims and all provincial/territorial R&D credits except those of Quebec and Alberta)5. According to the CRA's SR&ED Privacy Impact Assessment, 80% of all SR&ED claims are filed electronically (where Business Number, tax year-end, and Web Access Code or EFILE password constitute the legal electronic signature), while 20% are filed and entered manually at CRA tax centres31.
Statutory Reporting Deadlines (ITA Subsection 37(11) and Paragraph 127(9)(m))

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA, as detailed in the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025) and Guide T4088, the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred5:

items: Corporations: Because a corporation's T2 return filing-due date is 6 months after its taxation year-end, the corporate SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for example, June 30, 2027, for a December 31, 2025 year-end)16.

Individuals (Sole Proprietorships): Because an individual carrying on a business has a T1 filing-due date of June 15 of the following calendar year, the individual SR&ED reporting deadline is 17.5 months after the end of the calendar tax year (12 months after June 15)5.

Partnerships: Form T661 must be filed with the partnership information return no later than 12 months after the earliest of all filing-due dates for the returns of income of the members (partners) for the fiscal period31.

body.text: If the SR&ED reporting deadline falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or a CRA-recognized public holiday, a claim is considered filed on time if received by the CRA or postmarked on or before the next business day5.
Absolute Statutory Bar Against Late Filing or Extensions (ITA Subsections 37(11.1) and 220(2.2))

Under subsection 37(11.1) and paragraph 127(9)(m), if a taxpayer fails to report an SR&ED expenditure on prescribed Form T661 and claim the resulting ITC on Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) on or before the statutory reporting deadline, no amount may be deducted in the section 37 pool or claimed as an ITC for that expenditure5. Furthermore, pursuant to subsection 220(2.2) of the ITA (applicable on and after November 17, 2005), requests to waive or extend the SR&ED filing deadline under the general ministerial discretion provision in subsection 220(2.1) cannot be made5.
Three important clarifications in the January 28, 2025 SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy govern partial or subsequent filings5:

items: Partial Project Submissions (Question 8 of Policy): If a claimant files Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 on time for 15 projects, but submits the Part 2 technical project descriptions for only 10 projects before the reporting deadline, the CRA will not disallow the entire claim; the CRA will accept the 10 complete projects and disallow only the 5 projects whose Part 2 information was missing at the deadline5.

Use of Existing Section 37 Pool Balance: Deducting an amount already residing in the section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is not subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline, provided the underlying expenditures were originally reported on time on Form T6615.

Part 9 Claim Preparer Information: Omitting or amending Part 9 Claim Preparer Information on Form T661 is not subject to the SR&ED reporting deadline and does not invalidate the section 37 deduction under subsection 37(11), though it triggers the $1,000 penalty under subsection 162(5.1)5.

To claim SR&ED tax incentives, a claimant must file both Form T661 (to report the projects and calculate the section 37 and qualified expenditure pools) and Schedule T2SCH31 (for corporations, including Part 12 identifying the ITC deducted, carried back, or refunded) or Form T2038(IND) (for individuals)5. Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the CRA issued updated versions of Form T661 and its companion schedules in May 202610:

items: Part 1 – General Information (Lines 010 to 157): Claimant name (Line 010), total number of projects claimed (Line 050), contact details (Lines 100–125), and partnership information (Lines 151–157)31.
Part 2 – Project Information (Completed for Each Claimed Project):

Section A – Project Identification: Project title and code (Line 200), start date (Line 202), completion or expected completion date (Line 204—defined as the date the scientific/technological advancement was achieved, the date it was determined the uncertainty could not be resolved, or the date the project was terminated, at which point eligibility ceases), field of science/technology code (Line 206), new Line 207 requiring the 5-digit Statistics Canada Canada Research and Development Classification (CRDC) 2020 Version 2.0 Field of Research (FOR) code (RDF#####), continuation vs. first claim indicator (Lines 208 and 210), new Lines 212 and 214 for the Pre-Claim Approval tick-box and Case Number, and joint/collaborative work disclosures (Lines 218–221)10.

Section B – Project Descriptions: Line 242 (technological obstacles/uncertainties overcome), Line 244 (work performed in the tax year to overcome those uncertainties), and Line 246 (scientific or technological advancements achieved)31. (For projects designated as "classified information" for national security reasons by a federal agency, Section B descriptions must be placed on a separate sheet retained in the claimant's records and not sent with the claim, accompanied by an explanatory letter sent to the CRA Business Tax Incentives Directorate in Ottawa and copied with the return31).

Section C – Additional Project Information: Person who prepared the Part 2 descriptions (Lines 253–259), key technical individuals directly involved and their qualifications/experience (Lines 260–261), new Lines 262 and 263 requiring the names and SR&ED operating time percentages of the 10 most expensive SR&ED capital properties acquired after December 15, 2024, foreign salary claim indicator (Line 265), work performed on behalf of another party (Line 266), non-employee contractor names and Business Numbers (Lines 267–269), and the Project Planning and Contemporaneous Evidence Checklist (Lines 270 to 282)5.
Part 3 – Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures:
Section A: Method election—Line 160 (Proxy Method) or Line 162 (Traditional Method)31.

Section B (Allowable SR&ED Expenditures): Domestic SR&ED salary/wages for non-specified employees (Line 300) and specified employees (Line 305); permissible foreign SR&ED salary/wages for non-specified employees (Line 307) and specified employees (Line 309); prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year (Line 310); current-year wages unpaid 180 days after year-end (Line 315); materials consumed (Line 320) and transformed (Line 325); arm's length contracts (Line 340) and non-arm's length contracts (Line 345); equipment lease costs used ≥90% (Line 350) and >50% to <90% under Proxy (Line 355); Traditional overhead and other expenditures (Line 360); third-party payments (Line 370); restored SR&ED capital expenditures acquired after Dec 15, 2024 (Line 390); summing to Total Allowable SR&ED Expenditures (Line 400)10.

Section C (Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures): Subtracts provincial government assistance (Line 429), other government assistance (Line 431), non-government assistance (Line 432), prior-year SR&ED ITCs applied and/or refunded (Line 435), and proceeds from the sale of SR&ED capital assets (Line 440); adds repayments of assistance (Line 445), prior-year pool carryforward balance (Line 450), amalgamation/wind-up pool transfers (Line 452), and prior-year ITC recapture (Line 453) to determine the Amount Available for Deduction (Line 455), the Deduction Claimed in the Year (Line 460), and the Closing Pool Balance to Carry Forward (Line 470)5.

Part 4 – Calculation of Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes (Lines 500 to 570): Starts with Line 400; adds payment of prior-year unpaid non-wage amounts (Line 500), the Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 502), Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504), and qualified expenditures transferred to the claimant via Form T1146 (Line 508); subtracts provincial, federal, and non-government assistance and contract payments (Lines 513–517), non-wage current expenditures unpaid after 180 days (Line 520), contract amounts paid to non-taxable suppliers (Line 528), 20% of arm's length contracts on Line 340 and third-party payments on Line 370 (Line 529), prescribed expenditures not allowed by regulations (Line 530), other deductions (Line 533), non-arm's length cost adjustments (Lines 538–542), and qualified expenditures transferred by the claimant via Form T1146 (Line 544) to yield Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (Line 559); and adds assistance/contract repayments made in the year (Line 560) to yield Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC Purposes (Line 570)31.

Part 5 – Calculation of Prescribed Proxy Amount (Lines 810 to 860): Calculates the salary base for non-specified employees (Line 810 less bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits on Line 812 = Subtotal Line 814) and specified employees (Lines 850–860, applying the lesser of 75% of total salary on Line 852 and 2.5 × YMPE prorated on Line 858 = Total Line 816) to determine the Salary Base (Line 818) and the Prescribed Proxy Amount on Line 820 (calculated at 55% of Line 818 for all taxation years after 2013 pursuant to Regulation 2900(4); note that older editions of Guide T4088 referenced historical 2013 transitional rates of 65%/60%)11.

Part 6 – Project Costs (Boxes 750 to 758): Allocates costs on a project-by-project basis across Box 750 (Project title/code), Box 752 (Salary or wages, which must equal Lines 300+305+307+309 excluding Line 310), Box 754 (Materials, equalling Lines 320+325), Box 756 (Contracts, equalling Lines 340+345), and Box 758 (Overhead, equalling 0 under Proxy or Line 360 under Traditional)31.

Parts 7, 8, 9, and 10: Part 7 additional statistical reporting (Line 605 in-house expenditures performed in Canada, subtracting Lines 307, 309, 340, 345, and 370); Part 8 claim checklist; Part 9 Claim Preparer Information (Lines 935 to 975); and Part 10 Certification (Lines 165 to 175)31.

body.text: 7.3 Claim Preparer Penalties (ITA Subsections 162(5.1)–(5.3)) and Gross Negligence Penalties (ITA Subsection 163(2))
1. Claim Preparer Disclosures and the $1,000 Joint and Several Penalty (ITA Paragraph 37(11)(b) & Subsections 162(5.1)–(5.3))

Under paragraph 37(11)(b) of the ITA (effective since January 1, 2014), Part 9 of Form T661 must contain prescribed information for every "claim preparer"—defined in subsection 162(5.3) as any person or partnership who agrees to accept consideration to prepare, or assist in preparing, Form T661, explicitly excluding an employee who prepares or assists with the form in the course of their duties of employment31. Any paid external assistance (including arrangements described as coaching or technical review) falls within the definition of a claim preparer79. Part 9 requires disclosing the claim preparer's name (Line 940), Business Number or Social Insurance Number under section 237 (Line 945), billing arrangement code (Line 950), billing rate (Lines 955–960), and total fee paid, payable, or expected to be paid (Line 965); if no claim preparer was involved, the claimant must complete only Lines 935, 970, and 97531. Under subsection 162(5.1), if required claim preparer information is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, a penalty of $1,000 may be assessed per SR&ED claim, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally (or solidarily) liable31. Under subsection 162(5.2), a claim preparer is not liable for the $1,000 penalty if the preparer establishes a due diligence defence—having exercised the degree of care, diligence, and skill to prevent the false statement or omission that a reasonably prudent person would have exercised in comparable circumstances76.
2. Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims (ITA Subsection 163(2) & CRA Policy Updated January 28, 2025)

As detailed in the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025, replacing Application Policy SR&ED 96-05), subsection 163(2) and paragraph 163(2)(a) of the ITA impose a civil penalty on any person who knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes, participates in, assents to, or acquiesces in the making of a false statement or omission in an original or amended SR&ED claim5. The CRA bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities to establish that the false statement or omission resulted from more than a simple oversight or misunderstanding of the law5. The penalty is equal to the greater of $100 or 50% of the understated Part I tax payable (or overstated refundable ITC refund) reasonably attributable to the false statement or omission5. When computing the penalty, the CRA applies a Deduction Priority Rule whereby overstated amounts are treated as being deducted first from the section 37 pool or Part I tax (ahead of any legitimate available balances), and post-audit requests for offsetting discretionary deductions (such as additional Capital Cost Allowance) do not reduce the penalty calculation5. Furthermore, under the Proxy Method, overstating SR&ED salaries automatically inflates the overstated qualified expenditure pool by an additional 55% PPA, magnifying the 50% gross negligence penalty5.
7.4 Pre-Claim Approval (Launched April 1, 2026), CRA Review Protocols, and Dispute Resolution
1. Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026) and Free CRA Advisory Tools

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval program enabling businesses to have their planned work evaluated for SR&ED eligibility before incurring significant costs10. To be eligible to apply, the business must be a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a partnership, must have gross business income of less than $25 million, and must be in good standing with the CRA, and the project must not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim or involve issues currently under litigation13. A claimant may apply for pre-claim approval for up to 3 projects, with each approval valid for up to 3 years24. After requesting a Case Number and uploading the completed application and supporting documents through My Business Account, the CRA assigns a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), holds a 2-to-5-hour virtual or on-site meeting (mandatory for new claimants, optional for existing claimants in good standing) to review the state of technology, technological uncertainty, hypotheses, and planned experiments, and issues a written Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report within 8 weeks10. While there is no formal objection process if pre-claim approval is denied, projects granted pre-claim approval that are subsequently claimed on Form T661 (reporting the Case Number on Lines 212 and 214) are processed within an expedited 90-calendar-day service standard if selected for an expenditure-only review5. In addition to Pre-Claim Approval, the CRA offers the online SR&ED Self-Assessment and Learning Tool (SALT) (which does not save or share data with the CRA) and optional, free SR&ED Service Visits (made permanent on June 20, 2023)1.
2. Post-Filing CRA Technical and Financial Reviews (The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants, Updated April 20, 2026)

For standard refundable SR&ED claims not covered by pre-claim approval, the CRA's service standard is 180 calendar days from receipt of a complete claim (which the CRA aims to meet 90% of the time); non-refundable claims selected for review have no fixed service standard5. Once a claim is selected for review (via automated risk assessment or random sampling), it cannot be withdrawn because Form T661 and its Part 10 certification are part of the official income tax return5. Reviews are conducted collaboratively by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager [FRM]), assigned through the National File Assignment System and conducted primarily via videoconference (or via on-site visits granted on an exceptional basis) using the CRA Portals (My Business Account / Represent a Client) or the secondary Secure Drop Zone launched January 15, 20245. Under Application Policy SR&ED 95-04R (Conflict of Interest with Regard to Outside Consultants), if the CRA engages an outside scientific consultant, the consultant cannot prepare SR&ED claims or give SR&ED tax advice to taxpayers or have any competitive or financial conflict, and the claimant has the right to inspect the consultant's CV prior to the review and require reassignment if a conflict exists5. During the review meeting, reviewers interview the technical performers, conduct a virtual or physical tour of the premises, and examine the Lines 270–282 contemporaneous evidence; as the CRA guide explicitly states, oral statements during an interview are not a substitute for adequate contemporaneous documentation5.
3. Four-Stage Dispute Resolution and Appeals Hierarchy (Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns)
When disagreements arise during an SR&ED review, the CRA's Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns establish a four-step escalation path5:

items: Step 1 (Reviewer Discussion): Direct discussion and clarification of technical or financial findings with the assigned RTA and/or FR5.
Step 2 (Manager Escalation): Involvement of the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM) to review the facts and perspectives of both parties5.

Step 3 (Administrative Review – Form RC532): After receiving the CRA's written 30-day Proposal Package (and before the file is closed by the reviewers), the claimant may submit Form RC532 (Request for Administrative Review) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre at the Business Tax Incentives Directorate in Ottawa5. Forwarded within 3 business days to the local SR&ED Assistant Director, the Administrative Review evaluates whether the claimant received due process and whether the technical and financial reviews were consistent with SR&ED legislation and CRA policies (either maintaining the decision or ordering corrective reconsideration, such as assigning an independent reviewer)5.

Step 4 (Formal Notice of Objection and Judicial Appeal): Once the review is finalized and a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued, a claimant who disagrees with the determination may file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch, and subsequently appeal to the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal5.

Canadian courts have established a comprehensive body of binding precedent governing technical SR&ED eligibility under subsection 248(1), the evidentiary weight of oral testimony versus contemporaneous documentation, corporate control (de jure and de facto) for the 35% CCPC rate, and the definition of government assistance.

body.text: 8.2 Detailed Synthesis of the Judicial Doctrine
1. The Binding Force of the Northwest Hydraulic Five Criteria (Northwest Hydraulic, C.W. Agencies, and Kam-Press Metal)

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839), Justice Bowman established the five-step judicial test for SR&ED eligibility, which was formally endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 5087) and summarized verbatim in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393 at para. 17)42:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? (where "routine engineering" describes "techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field")42;
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?42;
Did the procedure adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?42;
Did the process result in a technological advancement?42; and
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and results kept, as the work progressed?42.

body.text: In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2021 FCA 88), the taxpayer argued that because the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) does not contain the words "scientific method" (and the CRA removed the phrase from its administrative glossary in 2015), the Tax Court erred in requiring adherence to the scientific method5. The Federal Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding that the Northwest Hydraulic five-criterion test—including the requirement that the procedure accord with the scientific method—has been repeatedly adopted by the Federal Court of Appeal and remains binding law87.
2. Witness Credibility vs. Legal Sufficiency: Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada (2026 FCA 175)

Decided on October 21, 2026, Tuna Temple Inc. v. Canada (2026 FCA 175, affirming 2025 TCC 183) is the leading contemporary appellate authority on the evidentiary burden in SR&ED appeals8. Tuna Temple Inc. claimed SR&ED deductions and ITCs for 14 projects across its 2005 to 2009 taxation years; the Minister disallowed 13 of the 14 projects8. At the Tax Court of Canada trial, Tuna Temple called a witness whom the trial judge explicitly found to be credible, while the Crown called no witness of its own and did not displace the witness's testimony on cross-examination8. Nonetheless, the Tax Court upheld the disallowance of all 13 projects because the evidence showed that for each project there was no hypothesis, the work relied on existing technology and processes, the approach amounted to trial and error rather than a systematic investigation, project records were inadequate, and the company failed to demonstrate a gap in the industry's knowledge8.

On appeal to the Federal Court of Appeal, Tuna Temple argued that its credible, uncontradicted witness testimony was sufficient to demolish the Minister's factual assumptions8. The Federal Court of Appeal unanimously dismissed the appeal with costs, establishing two vital litigation principles8:

items: Credibility Does Not Equal Legal Sufficiency: Believing a witness is telling the truth is legally distinct from finding that the content of their testimony satisfies the five Northwest Hydraulic legal criteria and refutes the Minister's assumptions8.

No Requirement for a Crown Witness: The Minister is under no legal obligation to call a competing technical or expert witness at trial, and may rely entirely on the taxpayer's own documents, direct testimony, and cross-examination to show that the statutory criteria were not met8.

body.text: 3. Contemporaneous Documentation and Holistic Project Evaluation (Les Abeilles, Joel Theatrical, Dock Edge +, Concept Danat, and CRL Engineering)
Canadian Tax Court jurisprudence strikes a nuanced balance on the fifth Northwest Hydraulic question (contemporaneous documentation):

items: In Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313), Justice Gaston Jorré allowed the taxpayer's appeal across four packaging-equipment projects, holding at paragraph 153 that "each project must be considered globally over the year, not each test individually" and confirming that while contemporaneous documentation is strongly recommended, its absence does not automatically bar an SR&ED claim if other credible evidence proves the five criteria94. Similarly, in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6) (and National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47 at para. 65), the Tax Court noted that a detailed written record is not an explicit statutory requirement in the text of subsection 248(1) and clarified that a "hypothesis" is simply "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial"85.

However, where documentary and time records are missing or superficial, taxpayers almost invariably lose in the Tax Court of Canada: in Dock Edge + Inc. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 11), the Tax Court dismissed a $72,000 SR&ED claim supported by only a few prototype photographs and three pages of handwritten notes, emphasizing that technological advancement requires advancing general understanding in the field rather than merely the taxpayer's own internal knowledge81; and in Concept Danat Inc. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 32), the Tax Court dismissed a $14,000 claim because employee hours were based on retrospective estimates rather than contemporaneous records81. Conversely, in CRL Engineering Ltd. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 65), the taxpayer won in full because it captured weekly system snapshots in a document repository and maintained an internal wiki logging data, methods, issues, and results as the work progressed81.

body.text: 4. Corporate Control Jurisprudence Governing the 35% CCPC Rate (Bagtech vs. Lyrtech RD)

Because the 35% enhanced refundable ITC for private corporations depends on maintaining CCPC status under subsection 125(7) (or qualifying as an ECPC after December 15, 2024), two Federal Court of Appeal decisions define the boundaries of de jure and de facto control52:

items: De Jure Control via a Unanimous Shareholders' Agreement (Canada v. Bioartificial Gel Technologies (Bagtech) Inc., 2013 FCA 164): Even though non-resident shareholders owned more than 60% of the voting shares of Bagtech, the shareholders had executed a valid Unanimous Shareholders' Agreement (USA) giving Canadian resident shareholders the contractual right to elect the majority of the Board of Directors52. Applying the Supreme Court of Canada's doctrine in Duha Printers (Western) Ltd. v. Canada ([1998] 1 SCR 795), the Federal Court of Appeal held that the CRA's administrative practice of ignoring a USA under the paragraph 125(7)(b) hypothetical shareholder rule was wrong in law, and confirmed that Bagtech qualified as a CCPC entitled to the 35% refundable SR&ED ITC52.

De Facto Control Trap (Lyrtech RD Inc. v. The Queen, 2014 FCA 267, affirming 2013 TCC 12): Conversely, even where a corporation is de jure controlled by Canadian individuals, if a public corporation or non-resident exercises control in fact (de facto control) through economic, operational, and financial dependence, the corporation ceases to be a CCPC and loses access to the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED credit (as also applied in MindReady Solutions Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 CCI 17)49.

body.text: 9. Comprehensive Audit-Readiness and Compliance Checklist for Canadian Claimants

To maximise federal and provincial R&D tax credit recovery while protecting claims against CRA audit adjustments in 2026 and subsequent taxation years, Canadian claimants should execute the following eight-step compliance protocol:

items: Review and Amend Post-December 15, 2024 Claims Under Enacted Bill C-15 Rules: For all taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, ensure that filings apply the $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit, the $15,000,000–$75,000,000 taxable capital phase-out (or the optional 3-year average annual revenue election), ECPC eligibility where applicable, and claim all eligible capital equipment purchases (Line 390), Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504), and equipment lease costs (Lines 350 and 355) incurred after December 15, 20244. If a 2025 claim was filed prior to Royal Assent using the legacy $3 million limit or omitting capital/lease costs, file an amended Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 within the 18-month statutory reporting window9.

Apply for Optional Pre-Claim Approval on High-Value Projects: Where gross business income is under $25 million, submit a Pre-Claim Approval application via My Business Account prior to or shortly after starting a new R&D project to obtain a written CRA eligibility determination within 8 weeks and qualify for a 90-day expenditure-only post-filing review5.

Maintain Real-Time Technical Evidence Mapped to Lines 270–282: Require project leads to document contemporaneously (via engineering wikis, weekly system snapshots, Git commit logs, Jira tickets, lab notebooks, and test logs) the baseline technological knowledge gap (Line 242), explicit testable hypotheses and experimental/analytical protocols (Line 244), and logical conclusions (Line 246), ensuring claims do not rely on uncorroborated oral testimony or trial-and-error rejected in Tuna Temple (2026 FCA 175) and Dock Edge + (2019 TCC 11)8.

Enforce Contemporaneous Project Time Tracking and Equipment Logbooks: Track employee hours by SR&ED project contemporaneously rather than using retrospective year-end estimates disallowed in Concept Danat (2019 TCC 32), and maintain operating-time logbooks for all capital equipment (Lines 262, 263, 390), Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504), and leased equipment (Lines 350 and 355)9.

Structure Specified Employee Remuneration and 180-Day Payments Before Year-End: Compensate specified employees (≥10% shareholders) via regular T4 salary rather than bonuses, profit-based pay, or dividends (which are excluded under subsection 37(9) and Regulation 2900(9)), file Form T1174 if a specified employee works across associated corporations, and pay all accrued SR&ED wages and arm's length contract invoices within 180 days of fiscal year-end under subsections 78(4) and 127(26)5.

Model the Proxy (55% PPA) vs. Traditional Method Election Annually: Because the method selection on Lines 160/162 of Form T661 is irrevocable once filed for the taxation year, perform an arithmetic comparison before filing—electing the Traditional Method only where provable, incremental overhead (such as segregated R&D cloud computing on AWS/Azure/GCP or heavy shop-floor utilities and employer benefit contributions) exceeds 55% of the PPA salary base5.

Sequence Provincial Filings (Especially Quebec's New CRIC) Before the Federal Claim: For Quebec R&D and pre-commercialisation conducted in taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, transition to Form RD-1029.8.CR (CRIC), capture eligible pre-commercialisation and capital outlays, and compute provincial credits first so that Lines 429 and 513 of federal Form T661 accurately deduct provincial government assistance6.

Enforce Strict Calendar Controls on the 18-Month Deadline and Part 9 Preparer Disclosures: Calendar the 18-month corporate deadline (or 17.5-month individual deadline) as an unwaivable statutory deadline under subsections 37(11) and 220(2.2), and verify that Part 9 Claim Preparer Information on Form T661 is complete and accurate to avoid the $1,000 joint and several penalty under subsection 162(5.1)5.
